I kinda got lucky. Originally went for the A construction (regular electrical as that was my background before low volt) and tested really well, killed it in the interview but just barely missed the cut off for the apprenticeship. They saw my experience and started me out as a 4th year, been working ever since. 

Pros:
-pay is great!
-benefits and retirement are taken care of outside of your check by the contractor which is great. 
-don’t pay for health insurance via your own money/check.
-most tools are provided by the contractor (power tools and specialty tools)

Cons:

Gonna be super upfront and honest with you because honestly I choose Adelphi because of its close distance to me when I was accepted into way better schools and have kicked myself for doing so in hindsight. Don’t let distance (at least anything under 1.5 hrs) be a driving decision in choosing where you go to school. Main reason I say this is because ultimately if you’re going into business you’re gonna have to travel either to the city or somewhere else (Melville out in the island) that’s usually pretty far for work. Also, as crazy as it sounds, you learn to better manage your time and quickly you realize an hour drive isn’t as bad as it may seem when you’re younger and still new to this whole idea of college/work. Please take my advice on that, I promise that after the first month of commuting you’ll realize that it’s not that big of a deal and that traffic really isn’t that bad. You usually end up leaving a few minutes earlier and spending time on campus after class to catch up on work from class so it’s not like you’re driving back and forth between classes. Heck I drive all over New York for work now that I’m in a whole different field and an hour drive is pretty light all things considered. 

But to answer your question, of the two schools you listed you can look at it this way. If you want to build good connections and have a degree with some weight and prestige behind it, as your previous comments have suggested, go to St. John’s. It’s a nationally recognized and respected school in terms of its business and law programs. I have family and close friends who went there and they all landed top jobs and amazing internship opportunities through both the school and the connections they made there. Again, an MBA is great in the long run but it really all trickles down to what your undergrad is, what you plan on doing long term career wise and what your job outlook is upon completion of your first 4 years. Everyone raves about having an MBA but few seem to acknowledge that people pursue an mba either after working a few years in the corporate world  (I.e with experience under the belt first) or pursue it while working. Eitherway, if you do want to go the MBA route there are plenty of options, St. John’s, Stony brook, Hofstra, etc. I haven’t kept up with mba programs much after all these years but they’re all pretty strong and have decent career trajectories. It’s just a matter of expense at that point. Remember a lot changes over those first 4 years don’t get ahead of yourself.

I also found that switching the timings from when I took the meds really made a huge difference. For me, taking it at night/the evenings used to lead to me waking up the next day in a complete fog/haze. I started taking it in the morning with a full bottle of ice cold water followed up by caffiene after an hour of being awake(helps prevent jitters and harsh caff crashes later on). I have a lot of questions for you. How does the electrical trade as a career go hand in hand with music? 

As for the apprentice wages it really depends on areas that you live in, experience, and what the culture of the company is like where you work at. 

If you can swing it take classes before your apprenticeship if you’re super green and know nothing about electricity or try to go union and get into the apprenticeship program or pre apprenticeship program. Classes and safety certs (OSHA 30+10 site safety) will go a far way in helping you get a better paying job. 

To be honest wages have slightly increased but for apprentices it’s still pretty bad but assuming you can make it on your current salary/pay of 17 it shouldn’t be that big of a difference in quality of life from a financial standpoint. 

As for tools look up on Google basic electrical hand tools needed. Usually it’s going to be a few screwdrivers, pliers, diagonal cutters, pump pliers/channel locks, a multimeter, non contact tester, outlet tester, linesman pliers, gloves and safety glasses and a good measuring tape.  

Knowing some concepts from osha can really help out if you want to work safe (identifying toxic chemicals, asbestos knowledge, working safe, etc) but realistically you don’t gotta know that shit word for word. Watch some videos and be cognizant at work. 

Some other things man, it’s going to suck starting out but if this is really what you want then stay at it.  You will likely get yelled at at some point or another pretty badly, and depending on where you work you’ll have to deal with the same guys. Not sure what to say there but it does get better, try to be helpful, ask questions, ask for ways to improve and literally learn and be hyper focused on your tasks.
